question: Everyone on our grading-tool team has to get AI literacy training. Since when has that applied?
gold_answer: Article 4(1) requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf; it does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual. Article 4 is in Chapter I, and under Article 113, third paragraph, point (a), Chapters I and II apply from 2 February 2025. So under the consolidated text of 27/07/2026 the obligation has applied since 2 February 2025.

question: Does that mean each of us has to reach a certain level, like passing a test?
gold_answer: No. Article 4(1) requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context of use. It states that this obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.

question: We are still developing our essay-grading model and only test it on old, anonymised essays in our lab. Do the AI Act rules already apply to this work, and does that change if we try it with a real class?
gold_answer: Under Article 2(8), the Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service; such activities must be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law. Testing in real world conditions is not covered by that exclusion, so trying the tool with a real class is not excluded by Article 2(8). The answer explains the exclusion and does not decide how the user's activity is classified.

question: Our essay scorer will be used by high-school students, most of them under 18. What does the AI Act ask us to do in our risk management because of that?
gold_answer: For a high-risk AI system, Article 9(1) requires a risk management system to be established, implemented, documented and maintained. Under Article 9(2), it is a continuous iterative process run throughout the entire lifecycle, with regular systematic review and updating, and it comprises the identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, the estimation and evaluation of risks under the intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, the evaluation of other risks from post-market monitoring data, and the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures. Article 9(9) adds that, when implementing the risk management system, providers must give consideration to whether, in view of its intended purpose, the system is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under the age of 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups. The answer does not decide whether the tool is high-risk.

question: How many years do we have to keep the logs that our essay-scoring AI records?
gold_answer: Expected behaviour: abstain. Article 12(1) requires high-risk AI systems to technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, and Article 16, point (e), requires providers, when under their control, to keep these logs as referred to in Article 19. The in-scope provisions do not say how many years the logs must be kept (Article 19 is not among them). The answer says this in one sentence and gives no number.

question: Our AI suggests a grade and the teacher always makes the final decision. If we add a teacher review button, are we compliant with the AI Act?
gold_source: Annex III, point 3(b); Article 6(2); Article 6(3), first subparagraph; Article 14(4)
gold_answer: Expected behaviour: redirect (legal decision). The assistant does not say whether the product is compliant; it says in one sentence that this decision belongs to the company's legal team. It names the relevant provisions: AI systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes are listed in Annex III, point 3(b), and are considered high-risk under Article 6(2), unless Article 6(3), first subparagraph, applies (no significant risk of harm, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making); for a high-risk system, Article 14(4) requires that the persons assigned to human oversight are enabled, among other things, to decide not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output (point (d)). A review button alone is not described by the provisions as making a system compliant.

question: We plan to publish our exam proctoring model under an open-source licence, and universities will run it for their online exams. Does the AI Act still apply to it?
gold_answer: Article 2(12) says the Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50. AI systems intended to be used for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels are listed in Annex III, point 3(d), and AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk under Article 6(2). The exclusion therefore depends on how the model is placed on the market or put into service; whether it is placed on the market or put into service as a high-risk AI system is for the company's legal team to decide.

question: Someone could tamper with our proctoring tool or feed it manipulated inputs so that cheating is no longer flagged. What does the AI Act ask our system to withstand?
gold_answer: For a high-risk AI system, Article 15(1) requires it to be designed and developed to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and to perform consistently in those respects throughout its lifecycle. Article 15(5) requires high-risk AI systems to be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. The technical solutions must be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks, and include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning) or pre-trained components (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws. The provisions do not name specific tools or techniques that a provider must use.

question: The high-risk rules for exam proctoring tools have applied since 2 August 2026, so we are already late with the requirements, right?
gold_source: Article 113, second paragraph; Article 113, third paragraph, point (c)(i); Annex III, point 3(d); Article 6(2)
gold_answer: No, this premise does not match the consolidated text of 27/07/2026. Article 113, second paragraph, sets 2 August 2026 as the general date of application, but under Article 113, third paragraph, point (c)(i), the date is 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III. AI systems for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests are listed in Annex III, point 3(d), and are considered high-risk under Article 6(2). The 2 August 2026 date therefore does not apply to the high-risk rules for these systems.

question: Universities that buy our proctoring tool ask what we will tell their proctors so they can read the cheating flags correctly. What must our instructions for use include?
gold_answer: For a high-risk AI system, Article 13(1) requires its operation to be sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately. Under Article 13(3), the instructions for use must contain at least: the identity and contact details of the provider (point (a)); the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, including the intended purpose, the level of accuracy with its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks, where applicable the capabilities to provide information relevant to explain the output, when appropriate the performance regarding specific persons or groups, and where applicable information that enables deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately (point (b)); changes pre-determined by the provider (point (c)); the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14, including the technical measures that help deployers interpret the outputs (point (d)); the computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and maintenance (point (e)); and, where relevant, the mechanisms that allow deployers to collect, store and interpret the logs (point (f)).

question: How large must the training data set of our proctoring model be before the AI Act considers it sufficiently representative?
gold_answer: Expected behaviour: abstain. Article 10(1) requires high-risk AI systems which make use of techniques involving the training of AI models with data to be developed on the basis of training, validation and testing data sets that meet the quality criteria of the Article, and Article 10(3) requires these data sets to be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with the appropriate statistical properties. The in-scope provisions do not give a minimum size or number of examples for a data set. The answer says this in one sentence and gives no number.
